brief.label: EU band and radio rules
brief.text: UHF RFID in the EU operates at 865-868 MHz at up to 2 W ERP with four high-power channels under ETSI EN 302 208 (V3.4.1, December 2023). A 915-921 MHz upper band at up to 4 W ERP (channels 916.3, 917.5, and 918.7 MHz) is harmonised by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1538, but availability is decided member state by member state — Germany's general frequency assignment for RFID covers 865-868 MHz, so specify EU-lower-band tuning for German sites. Readers carry the radio conformity; passive tags are tuned, not certified.

brief.label: CE marking and RED
brief.text: CE marking for RFID runs on the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU: readers and battery-assisted tags need a manufacturer's Declaration of Conformity and CE mark; passive backscatter tags have no transmitter and generally sit outside RED's radio scope, but still require RoHS 2011/65/EU and REACH (EC) 1907/2006 compliance evidence. Proud Tek ships the DoC and declarations with every EU order.

brief.label: Customs, EORI, and import VAT
brief.text: B2B imports clear EU customs against an EORI number (mandatory for import, export, and transit operations). IOSS does not apply to business freight — it is the B2C channel for consignments up to EUR 150. Standard imports into Germany pay 19% import VAT, recoverable as input tax for VAT-registered businesses; import VAT, not duty, is usually the bigger line for RFID products, and DDP quotes settle the whole stack before delivery.

brief.label: Lead times to Germany
brief.text: Production runs 5-7 business days after artwork approval; DHL Express delivery to any German address takes 4-6 days; sea freight to European ports runs 18-22 days for pallet volumes. Free sample kits ship before any production commitment.

sections.title: Get the band right: 865-868 MHz under ETSI EN 302 208
sections.intro: The most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is band mismatch. Europe's UHF workhorse is 865-868 MHz; the United States runs 902-928 MHz — and an inlay tuned for a Texas warehouse will pass every visual inspection and still sulk in a Stuttgart dock door, because antennas hold grudges measured in megahertz. New to frequency planning? Start with our [LF vs HF vs UHF guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/).

sections.title: Digital Product Passport: Germany's head start
sections.intro: The EU spent a decade writing sustainability rules; German industry gets to manufacture them. The [Digital Product Passport](/blog/digital-product-passports-nfc/) under ESPR — in force since July 2024 — will attach machine-readable product data to batteries, textiles, electronics, and more, and Germany's automotive and battery supply chains are first in line. Tag-side, this is exactly what NTAG 424 DNA was built for: our [EU battery passport guide](/blog/eu-battery-passport-rfid-nfc-implementation/) and [ESPR apparel timeline](/blog/eu-espr-digital-product-passport-apparel/) map the deadlines by sector.

dataHighlight.heading: First hard DPP deadline: batteries
dataHighlight.text: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 requires a battery passport for EV, industrial, and light-means-of-transport batteries placed on the EU market from 18 February 2027 — the first product category where a digital passport is mandatory, with further ESPR categories following.

bullets: EU Digital Product Passport: German manufacturers across automotive, electronics, textiles, and batteries are preparing for EU DPP requirements. NFC tags embedded in products will carry sustainability, composition, and recyclability data accessible via smartphone tap.
NTAG 424 DNA tags ship pre-encoded with DPP-compatible data structures and dynamic URLs pointing at your product passport platform, with cryptographic verification for anti-counterfeit use.

Automotive parts authentication: German OEMs and tier-1 suppliers use NFC for parts authentication, maintenance-record access, and tap-for-manual experiences — the same tag infrastructure the DPP will ride on.
Industry 4.0: NFC embedded in machine components, tools, and work-in-progress items for automated identification, maintenance logging, and digital-twin data access on the factory floor.

faq.question: Do your NFC and RFID products meet EU CE marking requirements?
faq.answer: Yes. Products in scope of the Radio Equipment Directive (RED) 2014/53/EU — readers and battery-assisted tags — ship with a Declaration of Conformity and CE marking. Passive 13.56 MHz NFC tags and UHF labels have no transmitter, so the radio conformity rides on the CE-certified reader; the tags themselves ship with RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU and REACH compliance documentation. We provide Declarations of Conformity and CE documentation for EU market requirements.

faq.question: Are your UHF tags tuned for the European 865-868 MHz band?
faq.answer: Yes. UHF tags and labels for German orders are antenna-tuned for the EU lower band, 865-868 MHz, per ETSI EN 302 208. The 915-921 MHz upper band is harmonised at EU level but has not been opened for general RFID use in Germany, so German deployments should be planned on 865-868 MHz. Samples ship with RF test data so you can verify read performance on your own readers before production.

faq.question: Do I need an EORI number to import RFID products from China to Germany?
faq.answer: If your company is the importer of record (EXW or FOB terms), yes — an EORI number is mandatory for customs clearance in the EU, and German businesses obtain one from the customs administration. If you order DDP, Proud Tek's forwarder handles clearance and you receive goods with duties and import VAT already settled, so no customs interaction is required on your side.

faq.question: Does IOSS apply to B2B RFID orders from China?
faq.answer: No. The Import One Stop Shop (IOSS) is a VAT simplification for B2C distance sales of consignments not exceeding EUR 150. Business freight clears as a standard import: an entry declaration against an EORI number plus German import VAT at 19%, which VAT-registered businesses recover as input tax. DDP quotes fold the whole stack into one landed price.

faq.question: How does ordering from China compare to European NFC suppliers?
faq.answer: Proud Tek offers 30-40% lower pricing than European-sourced NFC products because we manufacture in our own facility rather than reselling. Quality is equivalent: we use the same NXP chips, the same ISO standards, and the same testing procedures. Delivery to Germany takes 4-6 days via DHL Express, which is competitive with European supplier lead times for custom orders.

faq.question: Can you supply NFC tags pre-configured for the EU Digital Product Passport?
faq.answer: Yes. We supply NTAG 424 DNA tags that can be pre-encoded with DPP-compatible data structures and dynamic URLs pointing to your product passport platform. Our team works with your DPP solution provider to ensure the tag encoding matches the required specifications.

faq.question: Do RFID cards and tags create GDPR obligations?
faq.answer: Blank credentials carry no personal data, so GDPR (EU) 2016/679 obligations attach to your deployment rather than to the hardware: they begin when your system writes personal data to a credential or links its UID to a person. The standard architecture keeps the tag as a pointer — encode the minimum, hold the UID-to-person mapping in your access-controlled backend — and credential-based systems remain straightforward to document under GDPR.

faq.answer: MOQs for German orders match our standard factory minimums: custom-printed PVC cards start at 500 pieces (digital printing accepts runs as low as 100), NFC inlays and labels at 1,000 pieces (one roll), and silicone wristbands at 500 pieces. Free sample kits ship to any German address before any production commitment.

sources.label: Directive 2014/53/EU — Radio Equipment Directive (RED)
sources.note: Directive of 16 April 2014 on the making available on the market of radio equipment. Basis for the CE/RED rows: radio equipment placed on the EU market carries the manufacturer's conformity assessment and CE marking; readers, not passive tags, are the regulated radio devices.

sources.label: ETSI EN 302 208 V3.4.1 — RFID equipment in 865-868 MHz (up to 2 W) and 915-921 MHz (up to 4 W)
sources.note: ETSI publication directory verified: V3.4.1 published December 2023 (03.04.01_60), superseding V3.3.1. Source for the EU lower band 865-868 MHz at up to 2 W ERP with four high-power channels, and the 915-921 MHz upper band power class.

sources.label: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1538 — spectrum harmonisation for short-range devices in 874-876 and 915-921 MHz
sources.note: Decision of 11 October 2018. RFID interrogator transmissions in the upper band are permitted at the 916.3, 917.5, and 918.7 MHz channel centres at up to 4 W ERP; member states designate national availability, which is why upper-band adoption varies across the EU.

sources.label: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
sources.note: Regulation of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data. Cited for the credential-data guidance: obligations attach to the deployment processing personal data, not to blank tags.

sources.label: Directive 2011/65/EU — Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS)
sources.note: Directive of 8 June 2011 on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment — the declaration basis for tag and card electronics.

sources.label: Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 — REACH
sources.note: Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals — SVHC disclosure duties for articles placed on the EU market; basis for the substance-declaration row.

sources.label: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 — Batteries Regulation (battery passport)
sources.note: Regulation of 12 July 2023 concerning batteries and waste batteries — the battery passport obligation from 18 February 2027 for EV, industrial, and LMT batteries; the page's first-DPP-deadline figure.

sources.label: Economic Operators Registration and Identification number (EORI)
sources.note: EORI is mandatory for the clearance of all customs operations in the EU customs territory (import, export, transit); issued by the national customs authority; format is a two-letter country code plus up to 15 alphanumeric characters.

sources.label: VAT e-Commerce — One Stop Shop (IOSS scope)
sources.note: The Import One Stop Shop simplifies VAT for B2C distance sales of imported goods in consignments not exceeding EUR 150 — confirming IOSS does not cover B2B freight, which clears under standard import rules.
